Westeros news post 13834 FETCHED via the Wayback raw id_ capture after a live 403, and the Sean T. Collins 2011 essay reached from the link inside it and FETCHED live. Leigh Butler's reread FETCHED for all three named chapters: the Prologue and Bran I (AGoT Part 1, via Wayback after a tor.com 403) and the Red Wedding (ASoS Part 30, chapters 51-52, live at reactormag), plus The Hedge Knight Part 1 for the register comparison. The five-part 'The Prose of George R R Martin' series LOCATED IN FULL (parts 3 and 4 recovered from part 5's own description) but its TRANSCRIPTS ARE BLOCKED: the caption tracks are ASR-only and every timedtext route returned zero bytes (curl with a browser user agent, fmt=json3 and fmt=srv1, an in-page fetch from the youtube.com origin, and the innertube get_transcript POST), while youtubetotranscript.com sits behind a bot-verification interstitial I did not attempt to pass; claims from that series are therefore drawn from each video's own written shortDescription read raw from the watch-page JSON, and the transcripts are OWED to a later round. Other registers covered: Dunk and Egg (Butler's Hedge Knight reread, Attewell's essay and its comments, Adam Whitehead's Mystery Knight review), Fevre Dream (Bedford at SFFWorld, on phonetic dialect and on what is left unsaid), Wild Cards (Martin's own words on the mosaic form). Substantive sources per route: 5 from the named roster, 3 by bibliography chasing (the Collins link inside news 13834, the affix study cross-linked from the 2014 Books & Boots post, and the Atlantic interview from that study's footnote), 3 primaries chased from the Wikipedia reference list for Fire & Blood (Independent, Publishers Weekly, Tor.com via Wayback), and 11 by lateral search. Not found or thin: no scholarly close reading of Martin's chapter openings surfaced; Matthew Voice's corpus study exists only as a conference abstract with no published findings; the Times, Sunday Times and GQ Fire & Blood reviews are paywalled and were read only as quotations inside a fan-site round-up, marked relay and low confidence. 26 substantive sources read raw; discovery stopped when the last two lateral searches returned only pages already read or non-substantive. Every one of the 88 quotations below was re-checked as a verbatim contiguous substring of the fetched text, and none exceeds twelve words.

claims.quote: detail is necessary, showing not telling is necessary, and nothing is gratuitous

claims.claim: Martin says that two characters remembering one event differently is deliberate rather than an error.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, interviewed by Rachael Brown, The Atlantic
claims.quote: Two different characters may remember an event in two different ways

claims.claim: The Atlantic's introduction faults A Dance with Dragons for characters who use the same idioms regardless of class or continent.
claims.source: Rachael Brown, introduction to the Atlantic interview with Martin
claims.quote: too much repetition, unexceptional prose, and characters who use the same idioms
claims.confidence: high; this is the interviewer's framing, not Martin's own words, and it contradicts the per-speaker-register claims held by other sources in this sweep

claims.claim: BookPage reports that Maester Yandel's history in The World of Ice and Fire is presented as undeniably distorted.
claims.source: BookPage, 'George R.R. Martin: History is written in blood'
claims.quote: Maester Yandel has presented a history that is undeniably distorted

claims.claim: BookPage reports that Elio Garcia and Linda Antonsson read 10,000 pages of the novels to extract every reference to history, myth and legend.
claims.source: BookPage, 'George R.R. Martin: History is written in blood'
claims.quote: they pored over 10,000 pages of novels

claims.claim: A linguistic reading finds that low-born speakers address a noble as m'Lord while nobles addressing peers say my Lord.
claims.source: A.R. Rivera, 'A Brief Linguistic Exam of A Song Of Ice And Fire'
claims.quote: will use a contraction of a formal address, “m’Lord”

claims.claim: The same reading identifies the repetition of 'bastard' across nearby sentences as lexical cohesion tying the passage together.
claims.source: A.R. Rivera, 'A Brief Linguistic Exam of A Song Of Ice And Fire'
claims.quote: this kind of repetition is called lexical cohesion

claims.claim: The same reading reports a lexical density score between 4 and 4.5 for A Game of Thrones.
claims.source: A.R. Rivera, 'A Brief Linguistic Exam of A Song Of Ice And Fire'
claims.quote: A Game of Thrones has a score between 4 and 4.5
claims.page: section on lexical density and readability
claims.confidence: medium; the figure is cited to a third-party source the page does not fully identify

claims.claim: The same reading gives A Game of Thrones an Automated Readability Index score of sixth grade.
claims.source: A.R. Rivera, 'A Brief Linguistic Exam of A Song Of Ice And Fire'
claims.quote: The ARI score for A Game of Thrones is sixth-grade
claims.page: section on lexical density and readability
claims.confidence: medium; the page attributes the score only to 'medium.com'

claims.claim: The same reading characterises Martin's writing as a bare-bones functionality combined with archaic diction.
claims.source: A.R. Rivera, 'A Brief Linguistic Exam of A Song Of Ice And Fire'
claims.quote: a clearly defined, bare-bones functionality that uses not only archaic diction

claims.claim: A conference abstract announces a corpus of the first four ASOIAF novels rendered searchable in full for stylistic analysis.
claims.source: Matthew Voice (University of Sheffield), abstract 'Writing Westeros: a Corpus Linguistic Study', Nine Worlds Academia
claims.quote: the first four books of ASOIAF are rendered searchable in their entirety
claims.confidence: low; abstract only, no findings or figures are published on the page

claims.claim: Graham Oliver counts roughly twenty main characters and one source of tension introduced within the first five chapters of A Game of Thrones.
claims.source: Graham Oliver, 'How to Write Like George R. R. Martin', Fiction Advocate
claims.quote: a source of tension (Others) and 20 or so main characters

claims.claim: The same critic argues Martin pairs exposition with dramatic incident so that background arrives without stalling the reader.
claims.source: Graham Oliver, 'How to Write Like George R. R. Martin', Fiction Advocate
claims.quote: By pairing the exposition with the dramatic, you reduce the chances

claims.claim: The same critic calls Martin's use of meaningful nicknames extreme, describing it as overuse.
claims.source: Graham Oliver, 'How to Write Like George R. R. Martin', Fiction Advocate
claims.quote: his extreme (over)use of meaningful nicknames
